Derivatives of optimal solutions

Source: vignettes/solution-derivatives.Rmd
solution-derivatives.Rmd
library(optcompR)

How does the optimal solution move when a parameter changes? Duals answer this for the optimal value and right-hand sides. opt_solution_jacobian() answers it for the solution itself and for any parameter, wherever it appears: in costs, matrix coefficients, right-hand sides or nonlinear terms. Such derivatives are used in bilevel optimization, in learning with optimization layers, and for sensitivity reports.

The method

At a local optimum x^*(p) with multipliers y^*(p), the KKT conditions on the active set A are

\nabla_x f(x, p) - J_A(x, p)^\top y_A = 0, \qquad g_A(x, p) = b_A ,

where J_A is the Jacobian of the active rows and variables at a bound are held fixed. Differentiating with respect to p gives the linear system

\begin{pmatrix} H & -J_A^\top \\ J_A & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \partial x / \partial p \\ \partial y_A / \partial p \end{pmatrix} = -\begin{pmatrix} \nabla^2_{xp} L \\ \partial g_A / \partial p \end{pmatrix},

with H = \nabla^2_{xx} L the Hessian of the Lagrangian L = f - y^\top g over the free variables. The optimal value changes by \mathrm{d}f^*/\mathrm{d}p = \partial L / \partial p (the envelope theorem). Every second derivative is exact.

The implicit function theorem applies when three conditions hold at the solution:

  1. LICQ: the gradients of the active rows (and active bounds) are linearly independent;
  2. second-order sufficiency: H is positive definite on the null space of J_A;
  3. strict complementarity: every active inequality has a nonzero multiplier.

When the first or second fails the KKT matrix is singular and the function stops. When the third fails it warns, because the solution map then has a kink and only one-sided derivatives. The active set is held fixed, so the derivatives describe small parameter changes; a large change can switch the active set.

A quadratic program

Project the point (2, 1) onto the half plane x_1 + x_2 \le p. For p < 3 the constraint is active and the solution moves along its normal: \partial x / \partial p = (1/2, 1/2).

m <- opt_model()
x <- opt_variable(m, "x", dim = 2)
p <- opt_parameter(m, "p", value = 1)
budget <- opt_constraint(m, sum(x) <= p, name = "budget")
opt_objective(m, sum((x - c(2, 1))^2))
r <- opt_solve(m)
d <- opt_solution_jacobian(r, p)
d$solution
#>        p
#> x[1] 0.5
#> x[2] 0.5
d$objective
#>  p 
#> -2
opt_dual(r, budget)
#> budget 
#>     -2

For a right-hand side parameter the optimal value derivative equals the dual, as it must.

Compare with central differences of re-solves:

resolve <- function(v) {
  opt_set_parameter(m, p, v)
  r <- opt_solve(m)
  c(opt_value(r, x), opt_objective_value(r))
}
h <- 1e-5
(resolve(1 + h) - resolve(1 - h)) / (2 * h)
#> [1]  0.5  0.5 -2.0
opt_set_parameter(m, p, 1)

Parameters inside coefficients

Parameters may multiply variables. Here p scales one cost and one constraint coefficient at once:

m <- opt_model()
x <- opt_variable(m, "x", dim = 3, lower = c(-Inf, -Inf, 0))
p <- opt_parameter(m, "p", value = 1)
opt_constraint(m, sum(x) <= p, name = "budget")
opt_constraint(m, x[1] - x[2] == 0.5 * p, name = "link")
opt_objective(m, sum((x - c(2, 1, -1))^2) + p * x[1])
r <- opt_solve(m)
d <- opt_solution_jacobian(r, p)
d$solution
#>         p
#> x[1] 0.75
#> x[2] 0.25
#> x[3] 0.00
d$active
#> [1] "budget"     "link"       "bound:x[3]"

The third variable is at its lower bound and stays there, so its derivative is zero.

Linear programs

At a nondegenerate vertex of a linear program the solution is a fixed basis solution, a linear function of the right-hand side, and does not move when costs change slightly:

m <- opt_model("max")
x <- opt_variable(m, "x", dim = 2, lower = 0)
b <- opt_parameter(m, "b", value = c(4, 6))
cst <- opt_parameter(m, "cst", value = 3)
opt_constraint(m, x[1] + x[2] <= b[1])
opt_constraint(m, x[1] + 3 * x[2] <= b[2])
opt_objective(m, cst * x[1] + 4 * x[2])
r <- opt_solve(m)
opt_solution_jacobian(r, b)
#> $solution
#>      b[1] b[2]
#> x[1]  1.5 -0.5
#> x[2] -0.5  0.5
#> 
#> $objective
#> b[1] b[2] 
#>  2.5  0.5 
#> 
#> $active
#> [1] "c1" "c2"
#> 
#> $multipliers
#> [1] "solver"
opt_solution_jacobian(r, cst)$solution
#>      cst
#> x[1]   0
#> x[2]   0

Nonlinear programs

With a local nonlinear solver the multipliers are estimated from the stationarity conditions on the active set; the result records it as multipliers = "estimated".

m <- opt_model()
x <- opt_variable(m, "x", dim = 2, start = c(0.5, 0.5))
p <- opt_parameter(m, "p", value = 0.3)
opt_constraint(m, x[1]^2 + x[2]^2 <= 1 + p, name = "disk")
opt_objective(m, exp(x[1] - p) - 2 * x[1] - 3 * x[2])
r <- opt_solve(m)
d <- opt_solution_jacobian(r, p)
d
#> $solution
#>              p
#> x[1] 0.3549066
#> x[2] 0.3473396
#> 
#> $objective
#>         p 
#> -2.426877 
#> 
#> $active
#> [1] "disk"
#> 
#> $multipliers
#> [1] "estimated"

When derivatives do not exist

Two copies of the same active constraint violate LICQ:

m <- opt_model()
y <- opt_variable(m, "y", dim = 2)
q <- opt_parameter(m, "q", value = 1)
opt_constraint(m, y[1] + y[2] >= q)
opt_constraint(m, 2 * y[1] + 2 * y[2] >= 2 * q)
opt_objective(m, sum(y^2))
opt_solution_jacobian(suppressWarnings(opt_solve(m)), q)
#> Warning: Strict complementarity fails at c1 (active with a zero multiplier);
#> the solution may only have one-sided derivatives.
#> Error:
#> ! The KKT matrix on the active set is singular: the active constraint gradients are linearly dependent (LICQ fails) or the second-order sufficient condition fails, so the solution is not differentiable here.

A constraint that is active with a zero multiplier sits exactly at a kink of the solution map:

m <- opt_model()
w <- opt_variable(m, "w")
s <- opt_parameter(m, "s", value = 1)
opt_constraint(m, w <= s)
opt_objective(m, (w - s)^2)
d <- opt_solution_jacobian(opt_solve(m), s)
#> Warning: Strict complementarity fails at c1 (active with a zero multiplier);
#> the solution may only have one-sided derivatives.

Mixed-integer solutions are piecewise constant in the parameters and are refused. To differentiate within a fixed integer assignment, differentiate opt_fixed_relaxation(result), the continuous model with the integers fixed at their optimal values.
